title: Why Non-US Residents Are Getting Their LLC Bank Accounts Rejected in 2025 (And How to Actually Get Approved)
content:
# Why Non-US Residents Are Getting Their LLC Bank Accounts Rejected in 2025 (And How to Actually Get Approved)

You filed your LLC. You got your EIN. You followed every guide you could find online.

Then you tried to open a U.S. bank account and got rejected. Maybe more than once.

You are not alone. In 2025, non-U.S. resident LLC owners are hitting a wall at the banking step more than ever before. The rules have tightened, the compliance requirements have changed, and most guides online are still giving advice from three years ago.

This post breaks down exactly why rejections are happening, what banks are actually looking for, and the step-by-step path that gives you the best shot at getting approved.

---

## The Real Reason Rejections Are Spiking in 2025

Banks are not randomly rejecting foreign-owned LLCs. There is a very specific set of reasons driving the surge in 2025, and most of them come down to one word: compliance.

### FinCEN's Beneficial Ownership Information (BOI) Rules

Starting January 1, 2024, the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) rolled out mandatory Beneficial Ownership Information reporting under the Corporate Transparency Act. By 2025, banks are actively using BOI compliance status as a filter during account reviews.

If your LLC has not filed its BOI report, or if there is any mismatch between your registered agent details and your EIN records, banks are flagging your application immediately.

> **Note:** BOI filing is separate from your EIN and state registration. Many foreign-owned LLCs skip this step entirely because it is not always mentioned during formation. This single omission is killing more applications than any other factor right now.

### KYC (Know Your Customer) Requirements Have Gotten Stricter

Every U.S. bank is legally required to verify the identity of anyone opening an account. For non-U.S. residents, that process is significantly more complex. Banks now require a clearer paper trail connecting the foreign individual to the LLC, including:

- A valid foreign passport (often certified)
- Proof of address from your home country (utility bills, bank statements)
- An EIN confirmation letter (CP 575 or 147C)
- Your LLC's Operating Agreement showing your ownership percentage
- Articles of Organization from your formation state

If any of these documents are missing, expired, or inconsistently formatted, most bank compliance teams will reject the application without explanation.

### The "No U.S. Physical Address" Problem

Banks want to see that your business has some foothold in the United States. A registered agent address on your formation documents is not enough for many traditional banks in 2025.

They want a real business address, not a PO Box and not a generic registered agent suite. Using a virtual office with a real street address in the U.S. is now considered close to a minimum requirement when applying as a non-resident.

### Trying to Open the Wrong Type of Account

This is a tactical mistake that trips up a huge number of applicants. Retail banks (think your local Chase branch) are designed for residents with Social Security Numbers and local addresses. Walking into a branch in the U.S. while visiting, or applying online through a standard retail application, routes your application to processes that were never built for your situation.

The account types and application channels that actually work for non-residents are different, and most people do not know they exist.

---

## The Banks and Fintechs That Are Actually Approving Non-Resident LLCs

Let's get practical. Here is an honest breakdown of what is working in 2025.

### Traditional Banks: Proceed With Caution

Traditional banks like Chase, Bank of America, and Wells Fargo can work, but the process is inconsistent. Your approval often depends more on which branch you walk into and which banker you speak with than on your actual qualifications.

If you are going this route, here is what gives you the best chance:

- Apply **in person at a branch** when visiting the U.S. (do not use online portals)
- Bring a complete document package with every item listed in the KYC section above
- Ask specifically for a **business banker**, not a general teller
- Have a U.S. virtual office address already set up before your appointment
- Be prepared to answer questions about your business model clearly and confidently

Even with perfect documents, approval is not guaranteed. Some branches will help you, others will turn you away. It is frustrating, but it is the reality right now.

### Mercury Bank: The Top Pick for Most Non-Residents

Mercury is a fintech banking platform built with startups and remote business owners in mind. It is consistently the most recommended option for foreign-owned LLCs in 2025, and for good reason.

Key advantages:

- 100% online application, no branch visit required
- No monthly fees and no minimum balance requirements
- Built-in wire and ACH transfer support
- Integrates with Stripe, PayPal, Wise, and most major payment processors
- Specifically designed to accommodate non-U.S. resident LLC owners

> **Note:** Mercury is not FDIC-insured directly. Your deposits are held at their partner banks which carry FDIC coverage. Understand this distinction before depositing large amounts.

Mercury does still require solid documentation, and they will reject applications where the LLC structure or ownership information looks incomplete. A clean, well-documented LLC formation is still essential.

### Relay Financial: A Strong Runner-Up

Relay is another fintech option that works well for foreign-owned LLCs. It offers multiple sub-accounts within a single business account, which is genuinely useful for managing taxes, operating expenses, and profit separately.

Relay also accepts non-residents and does not require a Social Security Number, making it a solid alternative if Mercury declines your application.

### Wise Business: For Transactions, Not a Primary Account

Wise (formerly TransferWise) is not a bank, but it deserves a mention here because so many non-resident LLC owners lean on it. Wise Business gives you a U.S. routing and account number, which lets you receive payments from U.S. clients and payment processors.

It should not be your primary business account. Think of it as a receiving layer while your real bank account is being set up, or as a tool for moving money across currencies efficiently.

---

## The Document Stack That Actually Gets Applications Approved

Document preparation is where most non-resident applicants lose. Here is the exact document package you should have ready before you apply anywhere.

### Formation Documents

- **Articles of Organization** from your state (LLC filed in Wyoming, Delaware, or New Mexico typically performs best for non-residents)
- **Operating Agreement** clearly listing the foreign owner's name, passport number (optional but recommended), and ownership percentage
- **Certificate of Good Standing** from your formation state (some banks require this to be dated within 90 days)

### EIN Documentation

- **CP 575 letter** from the IRS confirming your EIN (this is issued once; keep it)
- If you lost your CP 575, order a **147C letter** by calling the IRS international line at +1 267-941-1099

### Identity Documents

- **Valid passport** from your home country (must not be expired)
- Some institutions require a **notarized copy** or an apostille, so check requirements before applying
- **Proof of foreign address**: a utility bill, bank statement, or government document in your name from the last 90 days

### Business Legitimacy Documents

- A **virtual office agreement or lease** confirming your U.S. business address
- A **business description**: a simple one-page document explaining what your business does, who your clients are, and how you generate revenue
- A **website URL** if available (having a live website increases approval rates noticeably)

> **Note:** Compile every one of these documents into a single organized PDF folder before you apply. When a bank asks for documents after your initial application, responding within 24 hours with a complete package dramatically improves your outcome versus trickling in documents over several days.

---

## Common Mistakes That Lead Directly to Rejection

These are the avoidable errors that show up repeatedly in rejected applications.

### Mistake 1: Forming Your LLC in the Wrong State

Not all states are equal when it comes to non-resident banking success. New York LLCs, for example, come with complex publication requirements and are viewed with more scrutiny by some compliance teams.

Wyoming, Delaware, and New Mexico are the three states with the most established track record for foreign-owned single-member LLCs. Wyoming in particular has become the default choice for non-residents because of its low annual fees, strong privacy protections, and straightforward compliance requirements.

### Mistake 2: Skipping the BOI Filing

As mentioned earlier, FinCEN's BOI reporting is now a live compliance checkpoint. File your BOI report at [fincen.gov](https://www.fincen.gov/boi) as soon as your LLC is formed. It is free, it takes about 10 minutes, and failing to do it is a compliance red flag that follows your LLC into every banking interaction.

### Mistake 3: Using a Nominee or Middleman Without Disclosing Them

Some services offer to put a U.S. person's name on your formation documents to make banking easier. This practice creates serious legal and compliance risk. If the beneficial owner (you) is not disclosed properly, you are potentially violating BOI regulations and banking fraud statutes.

Always structure your LLC with your own name as the member. Handle compliance directly. The short-term convenience of nominee structures is not worth the long-term legal exposure.

### Mistake 4: Applying to Multiple Banks Rapidly

If you get rejected once and immediately apply to five other banks in the same week, you can create a pattern that looks suspicious in banking compliance systems. Space out your applications, fix whatever caused the first rejection, and approach the next application with an improved document package.

### Mistake 5: Having No Business Activity When You Apply

Some banks want to see that your LLC has a reason to exist beyond just holding funds. Having even a basic website, an active service offering, or a few invoices ready to show demonstrates that this is a real operating business. Apply when your business has some visible activity, not the day after formation.

---

## The Step-by-Step Process That Works in 2025

Here is the complete sequence to follow from start to approved.

### Step 1: Form Your LLC in Wyoming, Delaware, or New Mexico

Use a reputable formation service or work with a professional who understands foreign-owned LLC requirements. Make sure your Operating Agreement is complete and reflects your ownership accurately.

See our full [LLC Formation Guide](/llc-guide) for a detailed walkthrough.

### Step 2: Get Your EIN

Apply for your EIN using IRS Form SS-4. As a non-resident without a Social Security Number, you must apply by fax or phone (not online). The international IRS line is +1 267-941-1099.

Once you receive your CP 575 letter, store it securely. You will use this document for every banking application you submit.

### Step 3: File Your BOI Report

Go to fincen.gov, complete your Beneficial Ownership Information report, and save your confirmation receipt. This entire step takes under 15 minutes and costs nothing.

### Step 4: Set Up a U.S. Virtual Office Address

Choose a service that provides a real street address (not a PO Box) in a U.S. city. Services like iPostal1, Regus, or Alliance Virtual Offices are commonly used. This address goes on your banking application as your business address.

### Step 5: Compile Your Full Document Package

Using the list in the previous section, gather every document and organize them clearly. Label each file so a bank compliance officer can identify it instantly.

### Step 6: Apply to Mercury First

Mercury's online application is straightforward, fast, and specifically designed for situations like yours. Apply with your complete document package ready to upload.

If Mercury approves you, you have a functional U.S. business account within days. If they decline, move to Relay as your next option.

### Step 7: Add Payment Processing

Once your account is active, connect it to a payment processor. Stripe and PayPal both work with Mercury and Relay accounts for foreign-owned LLCs. This is how you actually start receiving money from clients in the U.S. and internationally.

### Step 8: Keep Your LLC in Good Standing

Pay your annual state fees. File any required state reports. Maintain your BOI record if your ownership information ever changes. A compliant LLC stays bankable. A neglected one creates problems that follow you for years.

---

## A Quick Reference: What Banks Want to See

| Requirement | Traditional Banks | Mercury | Relay |
|---|---|---|---|
| U.S. SSN Required | Sometimes | No | No |
| In-Person Visit | Often Required | No | No |
| Foreign Passport Accepted | Yes (with caveats) | Yes | Yes |
| BOI Filing Checked | Increasingly | Yes | Yes |
| Virtual Office Address Accepted | Varies by Branch | Yes | Yes |
| Typical Approval Timeline | 1 to 4 weeks | 3 to 7 days | 3 to 10 days |

---

## What to Do If You Keep Getting Rejected

If you have tried multiple times and keep hitting walls, something foundational needs to be fixed before you apply again.

Work through this checklist:

- Is your BOI report filed and accurate?
- Does your Operating Agreement match the name on your passport exactly?
- Is your CP 575 or 147C letter available and current?
- Is your LLC in good standing with the state?
- Do you have a U.S. virtual office address on your application?
- Is your business description clear and credible?

If all of those boxes are checked and you are still being rejected, it may be time to get professional eyes on your situation. There are nuances in document presentation, LLC structure, and application strategy that are hard to troubleshoot alone.

Our [consultancy services](/consultancy) are specifically built for exactly this scenario. We work directly with non-resident LLC owners to identify what is blocking approval and create a clear path forward.

---

## The Bottom Line

Banking as a non-U.S. resident LLC owner in 2025 is harder than it used to be. But it is absolutely still achievable when you approach it correctly.

The people getting approved are not necessarily more qualified than those getting rejected. They are just better prepared. They have the right documents, the right LLC structure, the right address, and they are applying through the right channels.

Do the foundational work first, apply strategically, and you will get there.
